quote: The Bank would receive payment messages instructing transfers on the core ledger in anonymised form and would not know the identity of the payer and payee.
actor: CB (Bank of England as core ledger operator)
transaction_scope: standard online mode (platform model, pass-through wallets)
modality: conditional on issuance; PIPs anonymise personal data before sharing with the Bank (doc 3 p.70: data 'would be anonymised and not be considered personal data' from the Bank's perspective)
justification: The joint BoE/HMT Consultation Paper states that the Bank would receive payment messages in anonymised form and would not know the identity of the payer and payee. The paper also says the anonymised data would not be personal data from the Bank's perspective. That goes beyond a statement that the Bank would not use the data, and implies the Bank holds no routine key to identity. The 2024 Consultation Response confirms this: the Bank needs only anonymised settlement data, and legislation would guarantee privacy (doc 4 p.27–28).
counter_evidence: doc 4 p.28: The Bank commits to exploring technological options that would prevent the Bank from accessing any personal data through the Bank’s core infrastructure.

quote: Therefore, our proposal for the digital pound envisages that Payment Interface Providers would identify and verify users, but anonymise personal data before any sharing with the Bank.
actor: PSP (payer's PIP; payee's PIP for its own customer)
justification: Rule §6.5. Premise (i): PIPs hold the identifier-to-person mapping because they record user identity and do KYC (doc 3 p.57). Premise (ii): PIPs routinely handle the transaction record because they initiate the payments (doc 3 p.57), and the PoC records transaction data as viewable by payer's and payee's PIPs (doc 6 p.22, fn 7–8). Premise (iii): PIPs link the two in the same online mode, since they anonymise the personal data in payment messages before sharing them with the Bank (this quote). The TWP corroborates that aliases give no privacy from PIPs (doc 2 p.56).
counter_evidence: doc 2 p.21: PIP and ESIP access to transaction data within the CBDC system should be limited to the legal and regulatory minima

quote: In addition to law enforcement to fight crime (operating via law enforcement agencies engaging with PIPs under rules already approved by Parliament and not directly with the Bank)
actor: law enforcement agencies and competent authorities; also authorities for PIP failure and payment disputes
modality: lawful basis under Data Protection Act 2018 (s.31 law enforcement purpose); wallet providers may challenge requests (doc 4 p.43); data framework to be presented to Parliament
justification: The Consultation Response names PIPs as the holders that law enforcement would engage with, and states that this would not happen directly with the Bank. The CP specifies that agencies would access personal data from PIPs on a lawful basis in compliance with the Data Protection Act 2018 (doc 3 p.75). Because the PSP is explicitly named as data holder, the route is via_PSP.

quote: Our current thinking is that this functionality would not be available at launch, but we will continue to explore device offline payments and review this position.
transaction_scope: offline (deferred offline enabled in design note; device offline not at launch)
justification: The latest document on offline payments is a design note, which states it is exploratory and not a final decision. The note proposes deferred offline payments, which settle later via the ledger, without describing their privacy treatment. Device offline payments would not be available at launch. The offline experiment only tested capabilities (doc 12), and no adopted offline commitment with a privacy description exists, so F4 is unknown.
counter_evidence: doc 12 p.11: No transaction record: Devices did not store a transaction record, and payments were effectively anonymous

quote: Just like opening a bank or other payment account, some level of identity verification would be required when opening a digital pound
modality: unconditional (identity verification for any wallet; tiers vary only the level)
justification: The Consultation Response states that some level of identity verification would be required when opening any digital pound wallet, and that the digital pound would not be anonymous. The tiered access discussed in the documents still involves 'limited identity verification' (doc 3 p.73). That is KYC-lite with verification, not a route without verified identity. The requirement therefore covers all routes.
counter_evidence: doc 4 p.43: Tiered wallets would allow PIPs to offer less stringent ID requirements for low value digital pound holdings and transactions

quote: PIPs would be required to identify users to protect consumers against fraud and financial crime, as is the case with commercial banks today.
justification: The Consultation Response states that PIPs would be required to identify users. It adds that some level of identity verification would be required when opening a digital pound wallet. The CP describes PIPs carrying out KYC and AML checks (doc 3 p.57, p.76).
counter_evidence: doc 3 p.73: users might be able to open a basic digital pound wallet with limited ID

quote: Law enforcement agencies would only have access to users’ personal information in limited circumstances and where there is a fair and lawful basis – as is the case today.
actor: law enforcement agencies via PIPs; also authorities handling PIP failure and unresolved disputes (doc 4 p.29)
modality: conditional: limited circumstances, fair and lawful basis (Data Protection Act 2018)
justification: The documents provide that law enforcement can obtain person-attributable data in limited circumstances on a lawful basis. It would do so through PIPs and not directly from the Bank (doc 4 p.29). The Response also names PIP-failure management and payment-dispute resolution as limited scenarios where data held by PIPs is relevant to authorities. Online transactions can therefore be attributed afterwards under defined conditions.

quote: Programmable money would be both prohibited through primary legislation and technically impossible in the architecture.
justification: The Consultation Response committed that legislation would guarantee the Bank and the Government would not program users' digital pounds (doc 4 p.31). The 2026 progress update confirms that programmable money would be prohibited by legislation and technically impossible. Programmability by PIPs is permitted only with user consent (doc 3 p.83). Holding limits restrict amounts held, not the use of funds.
counter_evidence: doc 3 p.82: observe any restrictions (for example, maximum user holdings – see below)

quote: To promote innovation, choice, and efficiency in domestic payments
justification: This is listed as the second of two primary motivations in the joint CP. It is restated in the Consultation Response (doc 4 p.19) and in the 2025 design notes.

quote: financial inclusion and improving domestic payments resilience
justification: The CP lists supporting financial inclusion among the 'other motivations' for the digital pound, beyond the two primary ones. The 2025 progress update includes supporting financial inclusion among the assessment's policy objectives (doc 9 p.16).
counter_evidence: doc 3 p.91: The digital pound may have limited potential to accelerate financial inclusion in the UK.

justification: The CP foreword, signed by the Chancellor and the Governor, declares safeguarding monetary sovereignty as a benefit. The first primary motivation includes underpinning 'monetary and financial stability and sovereignty' (doc 3 p.28). Monetary policy transmission is explicitly not a motivation (Box F), but the sovereignty component of the flag is declared.
counter_evidence: doc 3 p.52: Remunerating the digital pound, either positively or negatively, to make monetary policy more effective is not a motivation

quote: The digital pound could improve resilience as an additional payment rail.
justification: Box D lists payments resilience as an additional motivation. The first primary motivation is to sustain access to central bank money as cash use declines, replicating the role of cash in a digital economy (doc 3 p.28, p.32).

No document declares AML/CFT or tax enforcement as an objective of the digital pound. AML compliance appears only as a design requirement (e.g. doc 1 p.23, doc 3 p.12), which the contract excludes as an objective.
counter_evidence: doc 1 p.23: Compliant: CBDC should be compliant with regulations around anti‑money laundering (AML)

quote: ensure that the UK remains at the forefront of innovation in money, payments and digital
justification: The Consultation Response foreword frames the digital pound work as part of efforts to keep the UK at the forefront of innovation. The CP foreword makes the same claim (doc 3 p.9). The CP also cites benefits to the UK fintech sector (doc 3 p.19).

quote: We consider there are two primary motivations:
justification: The CP explicitly names two primary motivations that 'go hand in hand'. Inclusion, resilience and cross-border payments are placed in a secondary 'other motivations' tier. The Consultation Response (doc 4 p.19) and the product strategy note (doc 11 p.5) repeat the two primary motivations.

value: (1) sustain access to UK central bank money as anchor for confidence and safety, underpinning monetary and financial stability and sovereignty (singleness of money); (2) promote innovation, choice and efficiency in domestic payments
quote: Our primary motivations for the digital pound are the availability of central bank
justification: The two primary motivations are listed on CP p.28. The 2025 notes rephrase the first as preserving the singleness of money (doc 11 p.5).

quote: We are continuing our evaluations of various ledger technologies and architectures
justification: The CP states that the platform model is agnostic and that the core ledger could be a traditional database or DLT (doc 3 p.57). The TWP only suggests that centrally governed distributed databases 'might' be more appropriate (doc 2 p.52). The 2025 update says evaluations of relational, NoSQL and DLT options are continuing. The Lab's centralised demonstration ledger is experimental only (doc 18 p.9), and a prototype ledger experiment is still ongoing in 2026 (doc 17 p.5).
counter_evidence: doc 5 p.18: the use of centrally governed, distributed database technologies might be more efficient and appropriate for the core ledger than DLT
